**Ch 030 draft**

1. **"Each mate or headsman, like a Gothic Knight of old, is always accompanied by his boat-steerer or harpooneer."** — The source continues to explain *why* this is relevant (because it sets up who the harpooneers are, and to which headsman each belonged). The transition sentence itself still parses, so this is borderline — but the gate test passes because a reader understands the sentence on its own.

2. **"But Queequeg is already known."** — This is a forward/backward reference that depends on Queequeg having been introduced earlier. In the source novel (Ch 003 onward), Queequeg was indeed introduced earlier. In the draft, Ch 029 and Ch 030 are the chapters provided, and Queequeg was indeed introduced in earlier chapters of the draft (the narrator's chapters about Nantucket and the Spouter-Inn). This is not a dangling reference — the prior draft chapters established Queequeg.

3. **"They called him King-Post on board the Pequod; because, in form, he could be likened to the short, square timber known by that name in Arctic whalers."** — The source adds "and which by the means of many radiating side timbers inserted into it, serves to brace the ship against the icy concussions of those battering seas." The draft cuts this but the matrix clause still parses. The reader knows King-Post is a timber and Flask resembles it in form. Not a structural failure.

4. **"Daggoo retained all his barbaric virtues"** — The source has "And never having been anywhere in the world but in Africa, Nantucket, and the pagan harbors most frequented by whalemen; and having now led for many years the bold life of the fishery in the ships of owners uncommonly heedful of what manner of men they shipped; Daggoo retained all his barbaric virtues." The "retained" implies a causal chain. In the draft this causal explanation is cut, so "retained" hangs without its explanatory scaffolding — but a reader can understand "retained his barbaric virtues" as a simple statement of character without the causal gloss. The gate test: not genuinely confused, just less ornamented.

5. **"an Ahasuerus to behold"** — This is used twice in the draft (once as "an Ahasuerus to behold" and once as "Ahasuerus Daggoo"). The name "Ahasuerus" is used as a characterizing epithet (the biblical Persian king, a type of imposing might) without any gloss. The source similarly uses it without gloss in both places. No difference introduced by compression.
